name: Frontload The First 30 Seconds
use_when: A YouTube video, short, tutorial, or talking-head edit needs to reduce early drop-off.
The opening contains silence, weak context, slow setup, or a promise that arrives too late.
The editor must decide where polish effort has the highest viewer impact.
A short needs a clear claim or visual reason to continue within the first five seconds.
The opener can be strengthened with a simple dynamic zoom, proof image, or face-focused visual inside the first 3-5 seconds.
avoid_when: A long-form invitation intro intentionally delays the promise with specific question loops and early trust closure.
A formal show, podcast, course, or social-series intro has passed the brand/proof/outcome gate and is capped tightly.
A breath, pause, or slow image is doing a clear emotional or comedic job.
The user explicitly wants a meditative or art-first opening.

timeline_pattern.effort_rule: Spend disproportionate polish on the first 30 seconds and especially the first minute because more viewers see it.
timeline_pattern.silence_rule: Remove accidental opening silence, dead air, or confusing hesitation.
timeline_pattern.value_rule: The opening should reassure viewers that the video will deliver what title and thumbnail promised.
timeline_pattern.five_second_rule: For feed-first shorts, the first five seconds should contain the claim, proof, question, or desire that makes the viewer stay.
timeline_pattern.three_second_motion_rule: A dynamic zoom, zoom-out, pan, or image/proof stack in the first 3-5 seconds can make a static opening feel active when the story supports it.
timeline_pattern.intro_bumper_exception: A formal intro can precede body content only when it quickly creates brand identity, external proof, or outcome expectation that the body alone would not create as fast.

motion.rule: Use motion only to clarify the opening promise or focus point; do not frontload random effects.
motion.dynamic_hook: Keep the first zoom crop-safe and tied to the face, proof, or curiosity object rather than treating zoom itself as the hook.

sound.rule: Opening audio should start cleanly, energetically, and match the intended tone. Keep intentional breaths only when they humanize or set the correct mood.

captions.rule: Opening captions should be immediately readable and should not cover the proof, result, face, or title-safe area.

color.rule: The first frame must reveal the subject, proof, or tone clearly; avoid a dark or unreadable opener unless mystery is intentional.

implementation.ffmpeg: Render a first-30-seconds review clip and contact sheet. Use silencedetect or waveform inspection to find accidental dead air.
implementation.remotion: Model the first 30 seconds as hook, proof, context, and continuation sequences so each has a visible job.
implementation.blender: Use animated intros only when they carry the promise faster than live footage or evidence would.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Trim opening dead air, add readable first-line captions, and preview at phone size before polishing later sections.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Use markers for first_frame, promise, proof, context, and drop-off-risk; review this range before the rest of the edit.

common_mistakes: Spending most polish on late sections few viewers reach while the opening remains slow.
Leaving accidental inhale, silence, or camera adjustment before the actual hook.
Making the first 30 seconds busy without making the promise clearer.
Using a formal intro bumper as a habit instead of proving that it improves trust or perceived value.
Opening with a claim that is energetic but unsupported by the rest of the short.
Adding a first-seconds zoom that crops out the proof, face, or captions.
Starting with product-first or mechanism-first explanation before the viewer's desired outcome is clear.
qc: Does the first frame create a reason to continue?
Does the video speak, show proof, or establish the promise immediately enough for the format?
Does the first five seconds contain a clear claim, question, result, or reason to continue?
If a first-seconds dynamic zoom is used, does it preserve the face, proof, captions, and action?
Is accidental dead air removed from the opening?
Does the first 30 seconds match the title and thumbnail promise?
If a formal bumper appears before the body, can the editor explain why immediate content would be weaker?
Are opening captions and overlays readable without covering the main proof?
